newsitem.title: USA: Clinton "pleased" by Hebron progress - White House.
newsitem.headline: Clinton "pleased" by Hebron progress - White House.

text.p: U.S. Mideast envoy Dennis Ross briefed President Bill Clinton on Thursday on the negotiations on Israeli troop withdrawal from Hebron and the White House said Clinton was "pleased by the progress."

The U.S. envoy reported to Clinton by telephone on the "progress of the work he has undertaken to help move the parties to an agreement on Hebron so that they can move on to the important work that lies beyond," a White House spokewoman said.

Mediation efforts by Ross, who returned on Wednesday after several days in the region, focused on a long-overdue Israeli redeployment in the last West Bank town slated for Palestinian self-rule under a 1995 Israel-PLO peace deal.

The top-level U.S. review of his effort came amid reports from the Middle East that Palestinian President Yasser Arafat expected a Hebron deal to be signed on Dec. 30 or 31. Palestinian officials who declined to be identified said Arafat announced the dates while briefing Palestinian lawmakers in Ramallah on the negotiations with Israel.

Clinton was "pleased by the progress" reported by Ross and gave the envoy "instructions on how to proceed when he returns to the region" over the weekend or early next week, spokeswoman April Mellody told reporters.

In a related development, a senior U.S. official denied a report by syndicated columnists Rowland Evans and Robert Novak that Richard Holbrooke might replace Ross. "There's no substance to that report," the official said.
Holbrooke, who as an assistant secretary of state negotiated the Bosnia peace accord in November 1995, has been working since February as an investment banker in New York.

The official, who asked not to be identified, also denied the columnists' claim that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bid for a meeting with Clinton had been rebuffed. The official said the two men were likely to meet early next year.

"There have been discussions about a meeting and they're ongoing," the official said. "The Israeli leader comes here quite frequently and it's likely that there could be a meeting in the context of that early next year."

Clinton and Netanyahu last met in October at an emergency summit in Washington called by the United States in a bid to keep the peace process from collapsing amid hostility between the Palestinians and Netanyahu's hardline Israeli government.
At that summit, Netanyahu and Arafat agreed to give top priority to a Hebron agreement and the two sides have been struggling to work out details ever since.
